Field studies of the Long-whiskered catfish, Iheringichthys labrosus, have provided detailed insights into its early life history. The species produces demersal, adhesive eggs with an egg diameter of approximately 0.7 mm, and the wet weight at birth, based on this size, is remarkably low at 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams]. Hatching of the yolk-sac larva occurs after an incubation period of 5.5 days [ab = 5.5 days] when the water temperature is consistently maintained at 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C]. Following eclosion, the prolarvae remain lecithotrophic, relying entirely on their yolk reserves for sustenance before the onset of exogenous feeding. During this critical phase, the small size of the newly emerged larvae makes them highly vulnerable to predation and environmental fluctuations, and the timing of first feeding is crucial for their survival and subsequent growth.

As individuals progress through the juvenile phase, they undergo significant growth until they attain sexual maturity. The standard length at puberty, marking the onset of reproductive maturity, has been recorded at 10.2 cm [Lp = 10.2 cm], which corresponds to a total length of 12.3 cm. At this stage, the wet weight at puberty is approximately 20.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 20.9 grams], a body mass indicative of the energetic resources that have been allocated to somatic development prior to the first spawning event. This size threshold is an important demographic parameter, as it dictates the minimum body size required for individuals to successfully enter the breeding population and contribute to the next generation within their natural riverine habitats.

The reproductive strategy of Iheringichthys labrosus is characterized by a relatively high fecundity schedule. At the optimum water temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], field observations suggest that females undertake four distinct spawning events per year [F_R_i = four distinct spawning events per year]. During each reproductive event, a single gravid individual can produce a substantial number of eggs, estimated at approximately 67,274.5 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 67,274.5 eggs per spawning event]. This high fecundity per event is a common trait among many freshwater siluriforms and serves to offset the high mortality rates experienced during the early yolk-sac larva and pelagic larval phases. The combination of frequent spawning bouts and large clutch sizes ensures a continuous supply of recruits into the population.

The ultimate size attained by adult individuals provides a clear picture of the species' growth potential. Based on the length-weight relationship for this species, the ultimate standard length reaches 36.1 cm [Li = 36.1 cm], which is equivalent to a total length of 43.5 cm. From this maximum length, the corresponding ultimate wet weight has been calculated to be 983.7 grams [Wwi = 983.7 grams], representing the peak body mass achievable under favorable environmental conditions. Reaching this asymptotic size requires a prolonged period of resource acquisition and minimal physiological stress. The substantial difference between the wet weight at puberty, which is only approximately 20.9 grams, and the ultimate wet weight underscores the extensive post-maturation growth that continues throughout the adult phase, a pattern typical of many iteroparous fish species.

The maximum lifespan observed for the Long-whiskered catfish is one of its most notable life-history traits. When held under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], the oldest documented individual survived for 8 years [am = 8 years]. This relatively extended longevity, compared to many other small-bodied catfish species, is hypothesized to be linked to their benthic, slow-moving lifestyle and the consistent thermal regime of their preferred deep-water habitats. The age at birth, at just 5.5 days [ab = 5.5 days], stands in stark contrast to this multi-year lifespan, highlighting a life-history strategy that involves an extremely brief early developmental period followed by a long, protracted adult stage where repeated reproduction is possible over many seasons at a temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C].
